item.title: 'Trust fund kid' vs. 'bigot': Personal attacks dominate Georgia Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The first debate for Georgia Senate on Thursday evening quickly devolved into a string of personal attacks and campaign talking points as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) wrestle for voters’ support in the closely-watched midterm race. The incumbent Democrat has maintained a lead over his GOP challenger in recent polling, but Republicans are still holding out hope to flip this seat in November. The candidates faced questions during the Atlanta News First debate in Atlanta about their stance on a range of issues, including artificial intelligence, border security, rural health care and agriculture. Repeatedly, Collins and Ossoff used their allotted time to criticize each other's family backgrounds and argue that their opponent was not fit to represent Georgia on Capitol Hill. Here are four takeaways from their first face off: Ossoff slams ‘bigot’ Collins The Democratic incumbent referred to Collins several times on Thursday evening as “the bigot congressman,” an insult he has repeatedly invoked on the campaign trail. Ossoff pointed to the lawmaker’s past controversial social media posts, including a sharing a video from the University of Mississippi in 2024 in which a Black woman is surrounded by white students who are mimicking ape-like motions and making monkey sounds. Collins captioned the post, “Ole Miss taking care of business.” “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said in reference to the post. The senator also accused the Republican of promoting “Neo-Nazi propaganda,” pointing to social media posts made by his son-in-law and a former staffer. “It’s not just that you hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted Neo-Nazi content online. It’s that you’re robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors,” Ossoff said during his response to a question about data centers. Collins responded to a moderator question about his son-in-law’s posts, saying he “condemned racism, anti-Semitism, hate.” “I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that too. It’s wrong,” he said. Collins attacks Democrat as ‘trust fund kid’ The Republican nominee called his opponent a “trust fund kid," arguing he's unable to understand the affordability issues faced by people in the state. Collins reupped this criticism in response to a debate question about financial troubles facing rural hospitals in the state. “You know the problem is, and Jon Ossoff won’t understand this because he doesn’t have to worry about health care,” he said. “He doesn’t have to worry about trying to buy health care insurance for his family. He never will.” Ossoff hit back, claiming his opponent “inherited a seat in Congress” during his closing statement. The Republican's father is Mac Collins, the late Georgia lawmaker who served 12 years in the House. Affordability concerns loom large Collins and Ossoff hit one another over their legislative record on affordability, as rising costs of living across the country remain top of mind for voters ahead of Election Day. The Democrat pointed to rising diesel and fertilizer costs amid the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariffs. “As we speak right now, it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of the Mike Collins-Donald Trump tariffs,” Ossoff said. “Just like it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of these high diesel prices. The Republican nominee placed blame on last year’s government shutdown, which he and other congressional lawmakers have accused Democrats of causing. “He shut it down, y’all,” Collins said. “Right when we were trying to get that emergency money out for Hurricane Helene so that our farmers and our small communities could repair and prepare for this year’s harvest.” Collins skirts question about 2020 election Ossoff put his opponent on the spot during Thursday’s debate about his support for President Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election, including in Georgia’s Fulton County. “Mike Collins is one of the most extreme members of Congress,” the Democrat said. “He’s a Trump puppet election denier. I want to hear if Mike still believes the 2020 election was stolen. What do you say, Mike?” Ossoff turned to face his opponent, who stared down at his notes before a moderator asked him a new question about The Laken Riley Act he introduced. item.title: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in for an hourlong debate Thursday. (USA Today Network; Reuters; Getty Images) GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity. Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs. Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks. “I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point. Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election. Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist. The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly . “I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.” Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise. “It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.” At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.” Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump. New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war . “I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.” El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households. “Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.” El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.” The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.” “I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.” El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer. “I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.” The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts , with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game. Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith . Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed . And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.” Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name. “Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.” He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/sparks-fly-abdul-el-sayed-mike-rogers-first-michigan-senate-debate-rcna599866

item.title: Who's Eric Deters? Kim Guilfoyle reportedly asked MAGA donor to pay $100,000 AmEx bill.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate and longtime ally of President Trump, has emerged in the national spotlight after an explosive report revealed his alleged text exchanges with Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, over her credit card debt. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle, ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and the former fiancé of Donald Trump Jr., allegedly pressed Deters to pay her $100,000 American Express balance without leaving a paper trail and, in exchange, promised to help him reach senior administration officials. Deters, 63, is a former attorney, businessman and conservative radio host who has spent years building connections within Trump’s inner circle. He declined to make the payment and has since publicly accused Guilfoyle of offering political access in exchange for large sums of money. Guilfoyle’s $100,000 request Guilfoyle’s dealings with Deters began drawing attention after the Journal obtained hundreds of text messages, emails and letters, detailing their relationship in a bombshell report. According to the outlet, Guilfoyle told Deters she needed the balance to be paid ahead of her July 9, 2025, confirmation hearing before the Senate. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in one exchange on the messaging app Signal, which was obtained by the Journal. The message was sent on July 3, 2025 — just days before her hearing. She then reportedly sent Deters instructions to wire $100,000 directly to her American Express account, suggesting the payment would not leave a paper trail. “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote. “Please.” Deters refused, telling Guilfoyle he did not have the money and could not make the payment without jeopardizing his marriage. The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle repeatedly urged Deters not to document their financial arrangements in writing, warning that doing so could threaten her ambassadorship. In an interview with ABC’s “Good Morning America” on Thursday, Deters characterized their relationship as a “quid pro quo,” alleging that Guilfoyle promised to use her political connections to help him if he provided the money. “She made it very clear, and the text messages make it very clear, she was so desperate for me to send that $100,000,” Deters said, claiming Guilfoyle offered to become his “ride or die in the Trump world” if he paid her. Guilfoyle’s attorney has since disputed the authenticity of the messages without identifying specific inaccuracies, saying the ambassador was owed money for previous speaking engagements and travel expenses — a claim Deters denied. Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to comment on the story, telling reporters while on diplomatic travel in Greece that he does not know if the allegations are “true or not true.” “Our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there,” Rubio said. His ties to Trump and the MAGA movement Deters has been an outspoken supporter of Trump since he first campaigned for president in 2016, promoting Trump’s candidacy as a morning radio host based in Ohio. He frequently declared himself “Trump today, Trump tomorrow, Trump forever,” according to the Journal. His connections to Trump’s family grew through Freedom Fest, a conservative gathering he launched in northern Kentucky in 2020 in opposition to COVID-19 mandates. The event attracted prominent figures in Trump’s inner circle, including the president’s sons Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr., as well as Guilfoyle, who became engaged to Donald Trump Jr. that same year before the couple announced their split in 2024. Deters told the Journal he paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over several years to speak at the event, along with $200,000 to Donald Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump. He also donated $125,000 to the MAGA Inc. super PAC, according to Federal Election Commission records. The event continued for several years, though its 2026 edition was canceled after organizers sold just six of the 100 available VIP tickets, according to Deters. In September, he said on Facebook that he is “never ever, ever, ever ever doing this event again.” After Trump’s 2024 election victory, Deters began seeking Guilfoyle’s help with several disputes involving federal agencies. One involved an Ohio spine surgeon named Abubakar Atiq Durrani, who fled to Pakistan after facing charges of performing unnecessary surgeries and defrauding insurance companies. Deters, who said he was advising attorneys representing hundreds of Durrani’s former patients, wanted the Justice Department to pursue his extradition. He also sought assistance with an IRS inquiry into a tax deduction connected to the sale of his interest in the family business. According to the Journal, Guilfoyle contacted then-IRS Commissioner Billy Long on Deters’s behalf and discussed reaching other senior administration officials. Deters also offered to pay her $1 million if she could arrange an interview with podcaster Tucker Carlson, hoping to draw attention to the Durrani case. The interview never materialized. Deters told the Journal that despite his financial contributions and connections, Guilfoyle failed to deliver on her promises, which included lobbying top Trump officials such as FBI Director Kash Patel and former Attorney General Pam Bondi. “She never came through on anything,” he said. Political career and legal controversies Deters launched several unsuccessful bids for political office, including for Kentucky governor and Congress, where he challenged Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in the state’s 4th Congressional District. The northern Kentucky businessman, who previously co-owned regional restaurant chain Snappy Tomato Pizza, is also a former criminal defense attorney. His legal career was marked by repeated disciplinary proceedings. In 2020, Deters was banned from entering a courthouse in Hamilton County, Ohio, after threatening on social media to burn it down. The Kentucky Bar Association also twice suspended him over misconduct, including making false statements in court proceedings and filing frivolous claims. The Kentucky Supreme Court rejected his effort to regain his license to practice law in 2021, with the chief justice describing Deters's approach to practicing law as “anarchy.” “Deters’ lack of self-awareness is utterly amazing,” the opinion reads. item.title: Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. military plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, when he faces a firing squad on Dec. 3 , a Pentagon official said. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said earlier Thursday the Pentagon planned to make the execution public. "He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Hegseth told Jack Posobiec on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Hegseth said the early December execution will take place at Fort Hood at 1 p.m. Earlier this week, the Trump administration approved the plan to execute Hasan . Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said on social media the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Hegseth and approved by President Trump. While executions are sometimes witnessed by small groups of people, including reporters and victims' family members, it is virtually unheard-of in recent history for an execution in the United States to be viewable by the general public. The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place in 1936, when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky, reportedly drawing a crowd of around 20,000. Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally." "There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said. "I think it's an acknowledgment of the gravity of the penalty to be imposed." He added: "In short, turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us." CBS News has reached out to Hasan's attorney for comment. A former Army psychiatrist, Hasan was convicted of murdering 13 people and injuring more than 30 in a 2013 court-martial. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was sentenced to death . Hasan's case could mark the military's first execution of an American service member since 1961, when a soldier was hanged for raping and attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl. It would also mark a rare use of a firing squad. Hegseth said "it hasn't been since World War II since we've done that," pointing to the military's 1945 execution of Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion . In state civilian court, the execution method was used in South Carolina three times last year, marking the country's first firing squads since 2010 . The federal government typically uses lethal injection in civilian death penalty cases, though the Justice Department said earlier this year that officials should consider other methods, including firing squads and electrocution. The decision by Hegseth comes after a lengthy appeals process for Hasan. He chose to represent himself at trial, and in an unusual course of events, he clashed with his own court-appointed standby attorneys , who worried that Hasan was intentionally seeking the death penalty. Hasan asked the Supreme Court to review his case in 2024, arguing the judge had violated his right to a public trial by clearing the public from the courtroom before discussing some of his issues with the attorneys. item.title: GOP efforts to lower gas prices derailed by Republican infighting
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republican efforts to reduce national gas prices in the weeks before Election Day were derailed in the Senate by infighting among GOP lawmakers and members of the administration who could not agree on how to ease consumers’ pain at the pump. The divisions within the Senate Republican conference over how to lower gas and diesel prices — even if temporarily — were driven primarily by geographic differences. Senators from oil-refining states shot down proposals from farm-state senators to ban the export of diesel or to loosen restrictions on the sale of E15 gasoline with higher ethanol content. “You’re talking about regional politics, and it gets bogged down in the politics of energy, and the fiefdoms around it,” said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and former Senate leadership aide. There were divisions that went beyond geography, too. Fiscal hawks torpedoed proposals to suspend the gas tax, even though their colleagues argued that doing so for a short period of time to bolster Republican candidates would have little real impact on the highway trust fund. And lawmakers had less flexibility on some possible actions because of the depletion of the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve by big drawdowns to stabilize market prices during the Iran war. The biggest problem, however, was that Republican senators didn’t see any proposal as likely to have a significant impact on prices before Nov. 3, when voters will decide which party controls Congress next year. “It is almost impossible to federally reduce gasoline prices for consumers because the levers of power that can be used have very little effect on the prices,” Bonjean said. The idea that appeared to have the most momentum was a proposal to impose a 90-day ban on diesel exports, which Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) began floating before a Senate Republican leadership meeting in mid-September. “We need to concentrate on affordability for this election. With diesel at $6, the best thing [President] Trump could do is follow what a Republican president did in the '70s and a Democrat president did in the '70s — when they were worried about the price of food, they put an embargo on soybeans and wheat — and [Trump] should put an embargo on diesel leaving the country,” Grassley told The Hill on Sept. 14. Trump embraced the idea, but it immediately ran into heavy resistance from oil-state senators and oil companies, who argued that it wouldn’t cut diesel prices but instead might even push them higher. “One thing we know for sure is that export bans don’t have a negative price impact, particularly with a commodity like that that’s globally traded and globally priced,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.). “If you restrict access to the global market for our diesel production, you literally disincentivize more diesel production in which case you end up with higher prices, lower supply,” he said. “You’re restricting your global supply, which has a global impact on prices.” Cramer warned that a diesel export ban “most likely would” raise diesel prices, especially in California and the Northeast, which import diesel from foreign sources. Sen. John Cornyn (R), who represents oil-rich Texas, dismissed the proposed diesel export ban as a “gimmick.” The White House in late September floated a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days, despite objections from Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who argued that “banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work.” Trump ruled out the idea last week before heading to Ohio to campaign for embattled Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio). Earlier this year, fiscal hawks such as Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) spoke out against a proposal introduced by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) to suspend the gas tax. The federal gas tax is 18.4 cents a gallon for gasoline and 24.4 cents a gallon for diesel. Hawley argued it would give American workers and families “immediate relief,” but Paul and other budget hawks warned it would blow a hole in the highway trust fund. Another proposal floated by farm-state Republican senators alarmed by the voter backlash to high gas prices was to allow permanent easing of restrictions on E15 gasoline, a fuel blend that includes 15 percent ethanol. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who’s up for reelection this year, touted E15 as a way to knock down fuel prices. “It would bring it down right now, some people think, as much as 30 cents a gallon — do voluntary E15 nationwide. It would be immediately available. It’s there now. It’s an American product,” Rounds told The Hill. “The president could do that today,” he said. Rounds also called for expanding refining capacity in the United States. But Republicans from oil-producing states argued that wider availability of E15 gas would hurt small- and mid-size oil refiners. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) declared his opposition to what he called the “year-round E15 mandate” after Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), announced in March that the Trump administration would expand the sales of gasoline with higher concentrations of ethanol over the summer. The fight will continue to play out during the lame-duck session of Congress after the Nov. 3 elections. Campaigning with Senate Republican candidate Michele Tafoya in Minnesota this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said he was optimistic about passing legislation to boost the availability of E15 gas in the stalled farm bill. “I intend and expect fully to get this done and get it across the finish line,” Thune said of the farm bill. “And it will include E15, exact version maybe to be determined.” Thune’s comments were reported by local radio station WZFG's “The Flag.” Even so, GOP strategists are doubtful that Washington can do much to impact the price of gas unless Trump finds a military or diplomatic solution to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has used to choke off much of the global oil supply. “It’s very hard to predict where gas prices are going to be after the election but one could put money down it’s still going to be high,” said Bonjean, the GOP strategist. He said, however, that prices could come down dramatically if Trump is able to eliminate Iranian threats to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz using serious “military intervention” — something the president has alluded to in recent days. item.title: The flu sidelines James Talarico at a crucial moment in the Texas Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has been off the campaign trail, sick with the flu. (Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty) The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now. But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days. His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend. While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care. It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date. “We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.” While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation. “He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.” At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event. “I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.” Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail. “After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.” Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him. Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem. “Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.” Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election. Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence. “It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.” To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention. At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail. “You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said Wednesday at a rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.” After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton. “He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social . It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though he’s not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media: “President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/james-talarico-flu-texas-senate-rcna602277

item.title: States urge residents to get ahead of Medicaid work requirements starting January
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
State health authorities are urging people enrolled in Medicaid to check whether they will remain eligible when new rules kick in that could leave millions of Americans without access. From Jan. 1, Medicaid beneficiaries in dozens of states will have to work, study or volunteer for at least 80 hours a month or meet a minimum income requirement to keep their coverage, among a series of new rules due to take effect. Many who are still eligible for the program risk losing coverage because of the "added paperwork" and "the hoops you have to jump through," Nate Crippes, a lawyer at the Disability Law Center in Utah, told the Associated Press . The Congressional Budget Office estimated in October 2025 that the new work requirement alone would leave about 5.3 million more people uninsured by 2034. A group of 25 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia sued to temporarily block the rules in June, saying it unlawfully narrowed exemptions for people with serious medical conditions. A federal judge denied the request in July . T he Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), the federal agency that administers the program, said in June that the changes were designed to promote "economic stability, self-sufficiency, and independence," and that they would help Americans build skills through work, education, job training or community service. Nevada, North Carolina and Pennsylvania are among the states that have issued guidance. Pennsylvania has urged residents to update their contact information and check whether they qualify for an exemption, as it mails notices to more than 700,000 expansion enrollees. Nebraska began rolling out the changes in May, Montana in July and Iowa will follow in December. Montana's grace period ended on Oct. 1, so enrollees there can now lose coverage for not complying. Here's what to know about what the new requirements are, who is exempt, how people can prove they qualify and what paperwork they'll need to keep their Medicaid coverage. What are the changes to Medicaid coverage? Starting Jan. 1, 2027, 40 states and D.C. will be required to introduce a work and community engagement requirement for adults covered by Medicaid's expansion to low-income adults — people ages 19 to 64 who are not pregnant and not enrolled in Medicare. In 2025, about 20 million of the 82.4 million people enrolled in Medicaid were in that group. Children, adults aged 65 and over and people who qualify through a disability or as low-income parents are not covered by the new rules. Enrollees in that group will need to work, be enrolled in school at least half-time, take part in a work program or volunteer for at least 80 hours a month. These activities can be combined to reach the monthly total, the federal rules say. They can also meet the requirement through income alone, earning the equivalent of 80 hours on the federal minimum wage — at least $580 a month in 2026. Income can count money from other people in the household, or from outside a job such as unemployment benefits. What do enrollees need to do? Rather than telling the state each month that they have met those requirements, enrollees will be required to prove that they met them for at least one month before the month they apply. This is also the case at renewal — which will take place twice a year — when existing enrollees must show they met it for one or more months between renewals. Some states, like New Hampshire and Indiana, have chosen to check more often. States have to check the records they already have first, like wage and unemployment data, SNAP and TANF files, Medicaid claims and school enrollment, before asking anyone for proof. Applications and renewal forms will include new questions and, in a few states, a separate portal for people to prove they meet these criteria. If a state cannot verify someone from its own data, it must send a notice of noncompliance, which must be answered within 30 days or its coverage ends. That notice has to explain how to show compliance or exemption, and how to reapply if they lose coverage. Who is exempt? Enrollees are exempt from meeting the requirement if they fall into one of these groups : medically frail, or have medical needs that significantly impair their ability to comply pregnant or postpartum a parent, guardian or caregiver of a child age 13 or younger, or of a disabled person a veteran with a total disability rating Native American and Alaska Native people a former foster care youth in a drug or alcohol treatment program in prison or jail already meeting TANF work rules, or in a household receiving SNAP without a SNAP exemption Those who are medically frail are facing significant changes. States must first look at 12 months of a person's Medicaid claims to determine if a person is medically frail. The condition must significantly impair a person's ability to work, study or volunteer. That 12-month history will not exist for someone applying for the first time, and may be thin for anyone who enrolled only recently. Those are the people most likely to be asked to prove it themselves. When the records cannot settle it, the new rules let states accept an enrollee's own account of their condition until the end of 2027. Starting in 2028, they can do that only once during a period of enrollment. After that, states must request documentation, which could include a doctor's certification, medical records, a disability award letter or a provider form. States cannot end someone's coverage solely because paperwork does not exist or cannot reasonably be obtained. How does this apply in my state? The requirement applies in the 40 states and the District of Columbia that expanded Medicaid to low-income adults. In at least six states — Arkansas, Idaho, Indiana, New Hampshire, North Carolina and Ohio — enrollees will have to provide documentation that they are medically frail rather than simply self-report, according to ABC News . Ten states never expanded Medicaid, and in six of those nobody is affected, because the group the requirement targets was never eligible there. The exceptions are Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin, which cover some low-income adults through waivers and whose enrollees are caught by the new rules. item.title: Christa Pike wasn't alone in her crime. What happened to the accomplices?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
While Christa Pike didn't act alone in the crime that landed her on death row , the two others involved in the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer met less severe punishments. Pike, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson were all students at Jobs Corps, a training program in Knoxville, Tennessee, when they lured Slemmer, a classmate, into the woods on Jan. 12, 1995. There, Pike and Shipp, a couple at the time, tortured Slemmer and bludgeoned her to death. They were both later convicted of the crime, while Peterson pled guilty and walked away with probation, according to court records. The grisly crime has garnered renewed interest after Pike's botched execution by lethal injection on Sept. 30. She was transported to a hospital and has since regained consciousness and is speaking , her attorney said on Oct. 7. Here's what to know about the other assailants in the case that's capturing national attention. Christa Pike accomplice Tadaryl Shipp serving life sentence Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder at a 1997 trial. He was sentenced to life and 25 years in prison, according to court and inmate records. Because Shipp was 17 at the time of the crime, he could not get the death penalty under state law. After Slemmer's murder, Shipp told police he "had dabbled in satanism since he was 10 years old," according to a 1998 appellate ruling. When he and Pike were taken into custody two days after the murder, they were both wearing pentagram necklaces, and Shipp told police he had "satanic paraphernalia" in his room at the Job Corps campus. Shipp told police he carved a pentagram into Slemmer's chest because he thought she could be "a satanic sacrifice." According to WATE and WBIR , Shipp was denied parole in October 2025. The 48-year-old will be eligible for parole again in 2031. Other accomplice, Shadolla Peterson, got probation Peterson, the other individual involved in the crime, pleaded guilty to being an accessory and received a sentence of six years probation, per court documents. She took a plea deal from prosecutors and received credit for 460 days in jail, according to a 1996 article in the Knoxville News Sentinel, part of the USA TODAY Network. While Peterson had initially been indicted on a murder charge, prosecutors said if the case had gone to trial, they would only have proof that she was present at the murder, not that she was involved in the killing, according to the article. The public defender who represented Peterson told the outlet at the time that she admitted to being present at the killing but denied taking part in the attack and did not know Slemmer was going to be murdered. What did Christa Pike do? On Jan. 12, 1995, Pike asked Slemmer to accompany her to a Blockbuster store before luring her into the woods, she told police. Pike – who had brought a box cutter and meat cleaver with her – and Shipp attacked Slemmer, bludgeoning her and eventually cutting her stomach and throat with the box cutter, according to court documents . During the attack, as Slemmer bargained for her life, Pike "told Slemmer to 'shut up' because it 'was harderto hurt somebody when they’re talking to you,'" she later told police, per court documents. Shipp also carved a pentagram into Slemmer's chest, and Pike – who told police she believed Slemmer was interested in her boyfriend – later showed off a piece of Slemmer's skull to a friend. Slemmer's body was found on Jan. 13, 1995. A Tennessee Grounds Department employee first mistook her body for the corpse of an animal because of how badly she had been beaten, according to court records . Born on Sept. 20, 1975, Slemmer was raised in Orange Park, Florida, but moved to Knoxville to enroll in Jobs Corps, according to court records and the Nashville Tennessean, part of the USA TODAY Network . More: Remembering Colleen Slemmer, the teenager killed by Christa Pike May Martinez, Slemmer's mother, told WBIR-TV that her daughter loved roller skating, computers and playing old games with her family. "She was a nerd," Martinez told the station. "But a good nerd." item.title: Democrats see a chance to flip deep-red states. But there's a catch.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats’ eyes may be bigger than their wallets. Democrats across a slate of deep-red states are clamoring for more cash to fight for Senate seats that suddenly seem within reach, with polling showing them competitive across a swath of normally impregnable territory from Kansas to Florida and South Carolina to Mississippi prompting a sudden bump in late-stage spending from outside groups. The party’s main campaign groups have already begun spending in Texas, another state they once downplayed that’s come seriously into play. But those same groups say they don’t have enough cash to protect the core battleground and also make significant investments beyond it — setting up Democrats for a series of difficult choices in the closing weeks of the midterms. “It’s very clear in the polling: If we get our message out, we're going to win. We're also not an expensive state to advertise in,” said Scott Colom, the Mississippi Democratic Senate nominee. “When it comes to Mississippi, we've been ignored for far too long.” Some Democrats see a generational opportunity to win seats in red states, driven by voters’ frustration with the economy that has hit rural and poorer red states particularly hard. And they’re starting to play around the edges. American Bridge PAC has pumped $2.1 million into Mississippi, where it is running ads targeting GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The state’s population is poor and mostly rural — two groups that have been particularly squeezed by high gas prices. Democrats have long dreamed it could become competitive, and Hyde-Smith didn’t reach 55% of the vote in her two previous Senate wins. The PAC also on Wednesday put $2.5 million into Florida, $630,000 into South Carolina and over $410,000 into Kansas as part of a $22.7 million investment on 6,000 billboards focused on higher costs spanning roughly 80 House and Senate races, the group said. “We are very aware that a durable majority means we are going to have to compete in totally new places, in states where we haven’t competed before,” American Bridge 21st Century President Pat Dennis told POLITICO on Wednesday. “And we also know that those changes don’t happen all at once, they’re investments over years.” But Democrats, despite polling well, are being massively outspent on the airwaves across the core battleground states. They’re already heavily investing in a swath of states President Donald Trump won in 2024 by double-digit margins — Alaska, Iowa and Ohio and, most recently, Texas. And they’re wary of spending big in states where major money chasing good polls have yielded very little in past elections. “Across the board, this is belt-tightening time and campaigns and committees need to make sure the money is being spent on seats to secure a majority,” said one senior Democratic operative working on Senate races, granted anonymity to candidly discuss spending strategy. “The stark reality is there aren’t the funds at the national level to invest in the next ring of states without putting the genuine toss-ups at risk.” That comes after a new group affiliated with former Vice President Kamala Harris’ super PAC dropped nearly $700,000 into Kansas last week to benefit Democrat Adam Hamilton, on top of nearly $5 million in recent spending from an outside group backed by a local attorney. A group that backs Democratic doctors and scientists running for office, 314 Action, has bundled roughly $3.6 million for Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) recently transferred $250,000 toward Angie Nixon in Florida, an expensive former swing state. Those aren’t huge investments; Democrats have spent or reserved over $100 million in Ohio alone since Labor Day, according to data from tracking firm AdImpact. But Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has included both Kansas and Mississippi in his pitches to donors and hosted a fundraiser for Colom over the summer. He told reporters last week that “we’re going to do everything we can in as many states as we can.” Senate Majority PAC recently told POLITICO it is “actively thinking” about whether to wade into Kansas — even as the group, which posted a record third-quarter fundraising haul, warned last week in a memo to donors that “the resources we have now” are not enough to “expand into new opportunities.” Republicans are legitimately concerned about Kansas , where high diesel and fertilizer prices driven by the war with Iran are hitting farmers and ranchers hard — outside groups have poured in more than $10 million into the state in recent days. Public and private polls show Hamilton tied or in the lead . Danedri Herbert, the Kansas GOP chair, said she was confident Republican Sen. Roger Marshall will win reelection but is relieved national groups are now paying attention. “I wouldn't want to leave it to chance,” Herbert said. “We're glad they're here and taking it seriously.” In a statement, Hamilton spokesperson Tyson Brody said Washington Republicans are “panicking” and “sending in millions to try to distract from Marshall’s record.” Some Democrats see good reason to spend more in some of the smaller long-shot states. Their money can go a lot further in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi — the same rationale they had when they invested in Alaska early this cycle but held off in Texas. "It's not a huge amount of money in these states. A little money goes a long way,” said Jaime Harrison, former Democratic National Committee chair and former Senate candidate in South Carolina. Democrats have been burned before by chasing these states. When Harrison ran for Senate in 2020, he raised $109 million . Polls showed a tight race before Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) beat him by 10 points. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) told POLITICO late last month that “we should be adding Mississippi onto that roster.” “It’s also an issue of optimizing of money, right? Mississippi is a smaller market. So you might be able to invest and actually have great turnout,” Gallego said. Gallego also said he hopes to campaign with Nixon in Florida, who’s a “really good candidate” facing a “very expensive” media market. But most Democrats aren’t opening their wallets widely for Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June before her upset against well-funded establishment pick Alex Vindman in the primary. Nixon’s campaign has spent $64,000 on streaming ads so far, while Vindman spent $2 million on TV ads in the primary. Nixon met with Schumer last week and “had a really great conversation,” said her campaign manager, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz. She also said DSCC leadership has been “very supportive of the race.” Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who chairs the campaign arm, held a virtual fundraiser for Nixon. In South Carolina, Andrews has posted healthy fundraising over a year into her campaign, which has helped her to blanket local broadcasts with ads for months against recently appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham. Polls have found a close race . Republicans are bearing down as well, putting $5 million for Graham in recent days. In a statement, a spokesperson for Andrews said the campaign has “the resources we need to share our message about lowering costs.” Kimberly Leonard and Lauren Fedor contributed to this report. item.title: Arizona candidate says she felt like a 'hypocrite' for not speaking up about reported rape
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democratic candidate for Congress who said she was raped while fixing a campaign sign in August, told ABC News on Thursday that she was motivated to speak up because of the arguments she was making on the campaign trail. "I was talking to some seniors about fighting for reinstating and funding the [Veterans Administration] and fixing Social Security, actually addressing the issues" amid federal government cuts or healthcare changes that impacted them, Greene-Placentia told ABC News Live anchor Kyra Phillips. "It just crossed my mind at that point -- like, wow, I'm kind of being a hypocrite because I'm saying I'm going to fight for Arizonans. I'm going to fight for these folks, but I'm not fighting for women who've been victims of sexual assault, and that's just not how I was raised," she said. "So afterwards, I told my husband and my team, I was like, this is really going to suck, but I have to speak up." ABC News - PHOTO: Arizona congressional candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia speaks to ABC News Live on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Greene-Placentia, a former truck driver who is running in the state's 8th District to try to unseat Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh, told Phoenix New Times, a local news outlet, in a story published Wednesday that she was attacked around 2 a.m. as she was walking toward a campaign sign in a parking lot north of Phoenix. She said she had been subdued and then woke up to find that she was being raped by an unknown assailant. Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped trying to repair campaign sign Greene-Placentia told the news outlet she reported the assault to the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office, which confirmed to ABC News that a report was filed on Aug. 31 and that there is an ongoing investigation, but said the office could not comment further on the investigation. She told ABC News on Thursday that she thinks it was a "crime of opportunity" and that she was not necessarily targeted, but she mentioned that her face is on campaign signs and "I'm pretty sure they knew who I was. Whether it was for political reasons or whatever, I mean, it was an attack on a woman, and no woman should be targeted, regardless of whether it's for political reasons or just because they're predators." It hadn't initially worried her to go out so late to fix campaign signs. "I mean, I have about 4 million miles across the country, and, you know, I've learned how to take care of myself ... it's just easier to do it [fix signs] at night. And usually I would go out with my husband or a staffer or a volunteer. But if I saw one that was just hanging by the rebar or somethin. ... I never heard [the attacker] coming," she said. "And it's frustrating to me because I like to think I have pretty good situational awareness, but obviously when someone deliberately sneaking up on you, it's hard to defend yourself." Greene-Placentia said she does not remember coming home and has little memory of the next day, although said there is video of her landlord in the driveway. "She saw me standing out there, and I guess I was just literally, like, staring off into space or something. And she's like, Bernadette, Bernadette, are you Ok? Are you Ok? And I just looked, you know, horrible." Courtesy Bernadette Greene-Placentia campaign - PHOTO: Bernadette Greene-Placentia is seen in this undated photo provided by her campaign. She said she did not say anything to her campaign staff at first, and took a few days before she told her husband. Asked what she wants voters to know about her in addition to her taking her story to Capitol Hill, Green-Placentia told ABC News she wants voters, including survivors of sexual assault, to know she was going to "fight" for them. "I want people to know that I'm going to stand up. I'm going to fight for you. I'm going to fight for everybody because -- I got into politics, I gave up a career I loved, because I felt like there weren't people like me, like the average American," she said. "Our voices were not being represented, and that's from the working class. That's from women that have been victims of sexual assault. That's our seniors, our veterans, our teachers, and they need to know that they have somebody that lives the same life they do, that has shared experiences, and will take that to D.C. and represent them fairly, transparently." She also said she understands where women who don't speak up about being assaulted are coming from, even though she used to be someone who was more judgmental of people who shared their stories. She brought up the 2018 hearings where professor Christine Blasey Ford accused then-Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh of sexual assault. Kavanaugh emphatically denied the allegations and was eventually confirmed to the court. "I am a little ashamed to admit that I was one of those people. You know, like during the Kavanaugh hearings, for example, I was like, 'Why did she wait so long? If he was out doing this to her, he's going to do it to somebody else.' But let me tell you, that is so hard to acknowledge to yourself that somebody took your power away from you, that they stripped you of your bodily autonomy, and you know overpowered you with physical strength, and you don't want to admit that." She added, "I was a truck driver. I was tough. I was in a male-dominated industry as an owner-operator and built up a small fleet. You know, how could I let this happen to me? I didn't want anybody to know. I just wanted to move on, and I can certainly understand why women don't want to tell that their story or what happened. But I also realized that as long as I don't say anything, then they maintain what -- they took that from me, and I wanted to take it back. And speaking out and speaking up for other women -- that is me taking it back." item.title: Long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. | Jae C. Hong “Home is the sailor, home from sea.” Robert Louis Stevenson penned that line almost 150 years ago — but on Thursday, those words read sweet and new to thousands of sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. After an almost 11-month deployment to the Middle East, the sea-weary aircraft carrier arrived at its homeport at San Diego’s Naval Air Station North to massive crowds of cheering, misty-eyed and flag-waving spouses, children, parents, friends and fellow troops. The massive ship played a pivotal combat role during the ongoing Iran war — setting a record-long deployment of more than 260 uninterrupted days at sea that included two extensions. The USS Lincoln arrived in San Diego Bay late Thursday morning under unseasonably warm skies. Scores of sailors and Marines, dressed in service dress uniforms, lined the carrier’s flight deck to the delight of awaiting loved ones. The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. | Karl Anderson The deployment’s historic length — coupled with reports of stark conditions during combat — brought wide attention to the USS Lincoln and its crew. And while the carrier is now far from the Middle East, the scrutiny of its 2025-2026 deployment will continue. Accounts of suicide attempts, food rationing, broken plumbing and mental health emergencies prompted Democratic lawmakers to call for a congressional hearing. President Donald Trump labeled reports of dire conditions about the USS Lincoln as “a CNN fake report” — and refuted that relatives of the Lincoln sailors had raised concerns about the carrier’s length at sea, saying the deployment was “not nearly long enough,” The Associated Press reported. And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in August that conditions aboard the Lincoln were “completely misrepresented.” But Navy leaders later acknowledged issues aboard a “city at sea” that thousands called home while underway. Meanwhile, experts told The Associated Press that the reported suicide attempts are a low number in a strike group of 6,000 sailors at sea for over 10 months. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., and Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., requested the congressional hearing following a Sept. 22 letter from Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirming that eight suicide attempts were made during the Lincoln group’s combat-heavy deployment. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect,” wrote Gillibrand, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. “That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.” Americans, she added, need hearings, accountability, and “a clear plan to protect our service members and prioritize American families.” Family and friends wait to greet the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier as it returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. | Gregory Bull Hegseth: A ‘generational mission’ for the USS Lincoln While the Lincoln sailors had to wait until Thursday to finally step on terra firma, Hegseth flew on a helicopter to the carrier Wednesday to get an early jump on the “welcome homes.” “I’m here today on behalf of the President of the United States to make sure you understand how deeply grateful we are — and how much we want to showcase and recognize the historic undertaking of this strike group,” said Hegseth. The secretary announced that Trump was presenting the USS Abraham Carrier Strike Group with the Presidential Unit Citation — the highest collective unit award in the American military. Hegseth also saluted the Lincoln carrier group’s “back of the baseball card” statistics that included almost 11 months at sea, two extensions in the middle of a combat zone, over 10,000 flights and 23,000 flight hours, 1.5 million pounds of ordnance dropped and 64 Iranian Navy ships sunk. “You were called upon by your nation for an important and significant and generational mission to ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” added Hegseth. “Theocratic regimes should never have access to nuclear weapons. President Trump recognizes that — and he called upon the Lincoln from day one to execute on that.” The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. | Karl Anderson The Iranians and the United States made a deal to share the ocean, he joked. “The Iranian Navy gets the bottom of the ocean — and the Lincoln gets the top.” Since the beginning of the Iran war, Hegseth has been frequently critical of the media’s coverage of the conflict. He once again scolded the press during his Wednesday visit to the Lincoln. “There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol — a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission,” he said. “And when I look at (the crew), and when I talk to your leadership. … I know it’s the exact opposite, which is actually what the media does so often.” The families and loved ones of the Lincoln sailors, added Hegseth, have also performed honorably during the long deployment. “When you greet your families tomorrow, just pass along my gratitude from the president and myself,” he told the troops. “Let them know that their long wait was in service of a righteous and historic mission. Thank them for their patience, for their patriotism, for their love, for their support and for pitching in on the homeland, which is never easy.” A woman watches as the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. | Jae C. Hong Lincoln’s sailors reflect on nearly a year at sea As the 1,092-foot-long vessel was navigating towards the U.S. mainland on Wednesday, many Lincoln sailors told the San Diego Union-Tribune that they were not always aware of the broad news coverage at home because Wi-Fi communication on the ship was sometimes limited. Roman Elliott, a 20-year-old mechanic’s mate, said, with a smile, “I learned to deal with it by playing cards. Lots of cards. “I am a little nervous about the (homecoming). It’s kind of like things were at the end of boot camp, when you’re finally free,” he added. “I’m looking forward to that.” Christian Webster, a 22-year-old aviation repair worker, had a different take, telling the San Diego Union-Tribune that he never thought he would see combat when he joined the military. “This is going to stay with me, knowing that I went through and accomplished what I want to do, and that I have gone far.” Meanwhile, sailor Steven Rivas learned firsthand the sacrifices that are often asked of American service personnel during times of war. His wife, Brenda, gave birth to their daughter during the historic Lincoln deployment. But Rivas didn’t find out he was a new dad for more than a week after Baby Evie’s birth because the Lincoln crew was not allowed to use Wi-Fi at the time to send messages. “I had no way to find out if there were any complications,” Rivas said Wednesday in a San Diego Union-Tribune interview. “It was just a waiting game for me to find out. When I finally did see pictures of (Evie) I, well, I cried. My wife said the birth was a real snap.” Rivas and his wife are not alone. The babies of scores of Lincoln crew members were reportedly delivered during the carrier group’s deployment. Sailors stand aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. | Gregory Bull This article originally appeared on Deseret News at https://www.deseret.com/u-s-world/2026/10/08/lincoln-navy-carrier-homecoming-iran-war/

Student leaders held a town hall to discuss fallout from the Jane Doe sexual assault case. - Surya Vaidy/CNN One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra. But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024. Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents’ home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn. Doe is increasingly scared for her own safety, Giuffra said in a phone interview with CNN on Wednesday as he detailed his client’s deteriorating mental state after an escalating series of violent threats. Officers pointed weapons at Jane Doe’s boyfriend, her brother and her father after receiving a bogus tip that “someone was killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening, he said. Death threats, doxxing attempts and an outpouring of anger online have also been levied at his client, Giuffra added. “I don’t think she’s in a good spot now,” Giuffra said. “She’s scared.” The public fallout from her allegations have rocked one of the country’s leading educational institutions. The university, its campus police force and the Tompkins County District Attorney’s office have each faced scrutiny over how they initially investigated her claims. Anger among students was palpable during a Wednesday sit-in on the Ithaca, New York, campus. Cornell students take part in a seven-hour sit-in protest on Wednesday. - Angelina Katsanis/Reuters Doe herself has been following media reports and social media posts on her case, Giuffra told CNN as he described a family reeling from a sudden and terrifying ordeal that punctured their sense of safety. “Before (this week), it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of,” he said. “Now it’s somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that’s pretty frightening.” Doe’s parents are furious after a fake tip to police, lawyer says At 7 p.m. on Tuesday evening, a police officer in Doe’s hometown was dispatched to respond to a disturbing call: A man had shot and killed his mother and then turned the gun on his sister. The information was bogus. But the officer, believing an active-shooter situation was unfolding, rushed to Doe’s home, where he saw a car backing out from the driveway, according to a police report from the incident obtained by CNN. As he apprehended the two men in the vehicle – later revealed to be Doe’s brother and her boyfriend – another figure emerged from the home’s doorway. “I’m the dad. What’s going on?” he yelled, according to the report. The man told police his daughter is Jane Doe of the Cornell case and that the family was “being threatened by numerous unknown people.” The swatting incident was an escalation in a series of threats to Doe’s safety that have roiled her family this week. The term “swatting” refers to false tips made to law enforcement agencies with the intention of having armed officers deployed to somebody’s home or place of business. “Luckily the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up,” Giuffra told CNN on Wednesday, relaying the events of the night. “(Doe’s) boyfriend got thrown on the ground,” and her father also had “guns put in his face,” according to Giuffra. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said. Police are now investigating the swatting attempt, and the FBI is also looking into the events, according to Giuffra. According to Doe’s lawyer and two police reports reviewed by CNN, police arrived moments after Doe received a separate phone call from somebody claiming to share a first name with one of the seven men she named in her civil complaint. According to her account to officers in the reports, Doe “began panicking” when she received the call, “because (her phone) wouldn’t stop ringing.” She informed officers about that previous call while they were at her house following the swatting tip. Before the night was over, Giuffra’s wife told him that she, too, had received a threatening phone call. “These people have done so much research into (Doe),” Giuffra said. It is not clear whether the separate threats cited in the police reports were connected. Giuffra said he was in contact with Doe and her family on Wednesday. Her parents are angry and she is terrified, he said. The lawyer shared with CNN an audio recording of a call he says was placed to his office on Wednesday afternoon. In the recording, a man identifies himself as “the person who called your client.” The man also is heard saying: “I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed.” Doxxing attempts also have taken their toll Tuesday’s swatting attack was an escalation of the potential dangers facing Doe since she filed her lawsuit last month, but it was far from the only threat she’s received, her lawyer said. Giuffra estimated that dozens of threats have been made against her since mid-September, when his client filed a 101-page complaint alleging she had been sexually assaulted and raped by several members of the Xi chapter of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity. The Chi Phi fraternity house on the campus of Cornell University. - Surya Vaidy/CNN Doe’s civil suit was filed against the university, the fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that members of the frat drugged and sexually assaulted her in October 2024 and invited other fraternity members in a group chat to join the assault. The suit also alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students, who all deny wrongdoing. Giuffra detailed to CNN another threat: a text message, sent to Doe’s phone on Monday, with three emojis depicting guns. Meanwhile, a handful of online personalities with large followings have led a campaign to uncover the identity of Doe, whose name was redacted in legal documents. One wrote on X to 347,000 followers in late September: “If you happen to know who this Cornell ‘Jane Doe’ is, get in touch and I would be happy to publish her name and identifying information.” He later claimed to have identified her and said he shared that identity online before deleting his post. Such behavior is known as doxxing, or sharing someone’s personal information or identity online without their permission. It has left Doe frightened and struggling to come to terms with the impact of the lawsuit, which has prompted outrage and scrutiny of how the university and its private police force initially investigated her claims. On Wednesday, Doe was “taping paper over windows in the house she’s lived at her whole life,” Giuffra said, “so people can’t see into her house to take a shot at her.” “I don’t get shook up very easily, but this shook me up. I didn’t want to have a body on my hands,” he said. “The dad is … concerned for his daughter. He can’t believe this has happened out of something where she’s just trying to stand up for herself and be heard,” Giuffra added. “But the parents are really strong people, and they’re going to protect their daughter.” Her career dream is ‘lost’ Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell’s prestigious Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and it had been her “dream” to attend the school, Giuffra said. Her complaint says she traveled across the country and arrived at the school with the same “hopes, expectations and trepidations of other high school graduates.” But she left the program without graduating after the alleged assault took place two years ago. Doe initially attempted to begin a career in New York City earlier this year, but after filing the lawsuit – “when everything hit the fan” – she instead returned to her family home, where she has been staying with her boyfriend, her lawyer said. “The dream is lost,” Giuffra told CNN, referring to her hopes of working in the hospitality industry. Instead, Doe has been hiding out at her parents’ home, where she has been following the intense media coverage of her case. “It’s kind of hard to switch it off,” Giuffra said. “She comes from a generation of people who are focused on social media.” CNN is not specifying the location of Doe’s family home at her lawyer’s request. She has been going on walks but otherwise spends much of her time indoors. She remains in contact with some of the friends she made at Cornell, Giuffra said. Cornell students Tuesday on the school's grounds in Ithaca, New York. - Surya Vaidy/CNN “She’s a little paranoid,” Giuffra said of his client. “If she’s out of (the) safety zone of her family, she just doesn’t seem to function well.” A few friends of the family know she has returned home and have been providing support, and Doe’s mother has taken time off from work to help look after her daughter, he said. Doe is also aware of the many messages of support that she has received from around the world since filing the lawsuit, according to Giuffra. Cornell, which recently appointed former acting US Attorney General Sally Yates to investigate the school’s handling of sexual assault claims, was the site of a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday to show “solidarity with Jane Doe,” according to flyers for the event. During a meeting with Cornell’s Graduate and Professional Student Assembly on Monday, university President Michael Kotlikoff acknowledged the mounting frustration across campus as more details and questions emerge about Doe’s 2024 allegations. “We’re all angry. I understand that anger,” Kotlikoff said, according to the independent student newspaper the Cornell Daily Sun. “People want easy answers to this.” The school’s president previously released a video statement promising further review of the case, saying it highlights “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.” “The students up there (at Cornell) have been overwhelmingly supportive, and it’s wonderful,” Giuffra said. “They’re trying to effect change, and bringing out to the light something that’s been going on for generations.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/08/us/cornell-jane-doe-threats-swatting

item.title: Curtis Flowers, tried 6 times for the same murders and freed after 23 years, dies at 56
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Curtis Flowers, a Black man from Mississippi who was wrongfully convicted multiple times when he was tried six times for the same crime by the same prosecutor, has died. He was 56. Flowers' family confirmed that he died Wednesday at his home in Winona, Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told CBS News on Thursday. No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers' legal team. CBS News has reached out to the coroner. Flowers' struggle with the justice system began in Winona, Mississippi, on a July morning in 1996, when the owner of Tardy Furniture, a bookkeeper, a delivery man and a 16-year-old were shot in the head execution-style. Flowers briefly worked at the furniture store that summer, but he was let go after he stopped showing up after only three days. Police questioned him after the murders, but didn't arrest him at the time. Flowers later moved to Texas to live with his sister, and he was arrested there in January 1997. He had no prior criminal history. McDuff previously called Flowers' case "unprecedented in the history of the American legal system." He told "60 Minutes" in 2021 that the first three convictions against Flowers were overturned "because of the prosecutor's misrepresentation of the evidence to the jury and because of his discrimination in the selection of the jury." The murder weapon was never found, and there was no DNA or fingerprints linking Flowers to the crime. In the first trial, an all-White jury convicted him after just an hour of deliberation. Flowers, then 27, was sentenced to death. His conviction was appealed and overturned. But he was tried five more times for the same crime by the same prosecutor. He had three more convictions overturned on appeal, in addition to two mistrials. The prosecutor was District Attorney Doug Evans, who in 2010 finally got a conviction to stick in trial six, and Flowers returned to death row. Then reporters at American Public Media's podcast "In the Dark" looked into the case. Their investigation led witnesses, including one who said Flowers had confessed, to recant their stories. "In the Dark" reporters and producers also analyzed decades of court data that revealed Evans had a history of excluding Black people from juries at a disproportionate rate. Across all of Flowers' trials, 61 of the 72 jurors were White. All 61 voted to convict. In 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Evans and the state of Mississippi had violated Flowers' constitutional rights and overturned his conviction yet again. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that there was a "relentless, determined effort to rid the jury of Black individuals." Six months later, Flowers was released on bail, leaving jail for the first time in 23 years. "And I'm telling you, I felt like I was floating. I was just ready to go," Flowers told CBS News in 2021.
